chapterTitle: Getting Started with Unity for XR Development
aiGenerationNote: Create a 15-minute interactive video tutorial. Begin by demonstrating the installation of Unity Hub and a specific Unity Editor version (e.g., 2022.3 LTS) with Android Build Support. Walk through creating a new 3D Core project. Then, systematically introduce each key Unity Editor window (Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, Inspector) with clear highlights and explanations of their function. Perform live coding/demonstrations of creating a Cube, Sphere, and Cylinder, then manipulating their Transform properties (position, rotation, scale) using both the Inspector and Scene view tools. screens.title: Getting Started with Unity for XR
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we introduce Unity as the primary tool for creating AR and VR experiences, and we orient you to the first steps you will take. Unity is a cross-platform engine used to build everything from simple AR overlays on phones to full VR worlds for headsets. You will learn what Unity Hub does, why you install the Editor with specific build support modules, and how starting with a 3D Core template gives you control as you learn. I'll show the core Editor windows — Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector — and explain how they map to tasks like placing objects, previewing a camera, and editing properties. We'll create simple geometry, attach a material, and manipulate transforms so you can feel confident moving in 3D space. This orientation matters because the early choices — which Editor version you use, which build supports you include, and whether you edit in Scene view or Game view — shape your workflow and reduce platform friction later. As a concrete example, including Android Build Support up front lets you deploy directly to many mobile AR and standalone headsets later without reinstalling. Notice a common misconception: the Game view is a preview, not the place to edit scene layout. By the end you'll know where to start, what steps to take first, and how to avoid the typical setup mistakes that cost time. How will you apply this setup to your first XR prototype?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives describe the practical skills you will build. First, you will understand why Unity is preferred for AR and VR: its cross-platform editor, package ecosystem, and component model make it effective for XR prototyping and production. Second, you will learn to navigate Unity Hub and create a 3D Core project, which sets up the project folder and initial scene. Third, you will identify the Editor's core windows — Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector — and know which window to use for each task. Fourth, you will practice manipulating GameObjects with translation, rotation, and scaling, and you'll understand how GameObjects and Components relate so you can attach behaviors through scripts or built-in modules. Each objective is framed for action: you will demonstrate these skills by creating a simple 3D scene and applying transforms and materials. A common misconception is that Unity's Editor is only for games; in fact, the same tools map directly to AR overlays and VR experiences. By the end you will not only know what each window does, but also why it matters and how to apply these capabilities to a real XR prototype.

screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on practice and troubleshooting. You will practice creating a Cube, Sphere, and Cylinder and setting their Transform properties exactly as shown. You'll learn to create a Material asset and apply colors using the Inspector. Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Practice Outcomes
Hands-on checklist
  1. Create Cube, Sphere, Cylinder in Hierarchy.
  2. Set transforms: positions, rotation, and scale per instructions.

screens.title: Why Unity is a good choice for XR
screens.narratorSegment: Unity is a cross-platform game engine with an editor designed for building interactive 3D content. Saying that Unity is 'good for XR' means it provides a unified workflow for creating scenes, composing assets, and deploying to multiple targets. Practically, that matters because AR and VR projects must run on devices with different operating systems, input systems, and performance constraints. For example, you might prototype an AR overlay on Android and later target a standalone headset. Unity's package ecosystem and community assets accelerate that transition. A concrete example: if you add Android Build Support during Editor installation, you can deploy the same scene to many mobile devices without reinstalling the Editor. A common misconception is that Unity is only for games. In reality, its component-based architecture, render pipeline, and XR toolkits support applications across visualization, simulation, training, and spatial UI. Another pitfall is assuming Unity automates platform differences; it does not. You still configure input, performance budgets, and platform-specific build settings. Key takeaway: Unity gives you a consistent authoring environment and reusable components, but you must make explicit platform choices early to avoid reinstalling or incompatible builds. Consider: which target device do you plan to test on first, and what build support will that require?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Why Unity
Definition
Unity is an integrated environment for building interactive 3D applications and deploying them across platforms.
Cross-platform
Write once, configure for multiple targets using build support modules.
Component architecture
Compose behavior by attaching components to GameObjects.
Ecosystem
Packages and community assets speed development.
Common misconception
Unity fixes platform differences automatically. It does not. You still configure input and build settings per target.
Concrete example
Install Android Build Support with the Editor so you can deploy the same project to mobile AR and standalone headsets without reinstalling.
Why this matters
Early platform choices reduce rework and keep your prototype deployable to the devices you care about.
Key Takeaway

Unity gives you a unified authoring environment and reusable components, but plan your targets and build support early.

screens.title: Unity Hub and installing the Editor
screens.narratorSegment: Unity Hub is a small desktop manager that organizes Unity Editor versions, project folders, and learning resources. Think of it as a control center: you use it to install specific Editor versions and add modules like Android Build Support or Universal Windows Platform support. The process begins with installing Unity Hub, signing in, and selecting an Editor version to install. When you choose an Editor, include the build support modules for the platforms you expect to target. For example, if you plan to build mobile AR or deploy to a Quest headset, include Android Build Support up front. A concrete step: after Hub installation, click New Project, select the 3D Core template, give the project a name, and choose a location. A frequent beginner mistake is installing a single Editor version without necessary modules and then being blocked when trying to build. You can add modules later, but it interrupts flow. Another misconception is that the Hub is optional; while you can run the Editor standalone, Hub provides version control and project organization that prevents version mismatch problems. Takeaway: use Hub to create a named project tied to a specific Editor version and include the right build modules at install time so you avoid reinstalling later.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Unity Hub
Install & configure
Use Hub to install Editor versions and add build support modules for your target devices.
1
Install Unity Hub
Sign in and open the installs tab to pick an Editor version.
2
Choose build support
Select Android Build Support for mobile AR and Quest builds; select UWP for HoloLens or Windows VR.
3
Create a project
Pick 3D Core, name the project, and choose a safe folder location.
Concrete example
If you're testing on an Android phone or Quest, include Android Build Support and the required SDK tools during Editor install so you can build and deploy immediately.
Pitfall to avoid
Installing the Editor without the needed build modules forces you to reinstall or add modules later, which interrupts your workflow.
Key Takeaway

Use Unity Hub to manage versions and include platform modules now to keep your project deployable.

screens.title: Create a new 3D Core project
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a new 3D Core project is your first hands-on step. From Unity Hub, click New Project and choose the 3D Core template; this template sets up a blank scene with default lighting and a main camera so you can focus on objects and transforms. Name the project clearly and choose a folder where you want your assets to live. After creating the project, Unity will open the Editor and present a Scene with a Main Camera and a Directional Light already in the Hierarchy. A concrete example: name your project "XR_First_Scene" and pick a dedicated folder in your Documents area to avoid mixing experimental files. A common beginner error is creating projects in temporary or synced folders that cause file locking or version issues. Also, avoid enabling experimental preview packages during initial setup; they can introduce instability. After the project is created, save the default scene (File > Save Scene) and give it a name, for example "MainScene". This habit prevents losing changes and makes your project portable. Final takeaway: a named project with a saved initial scene and appropriate folder structure prevents confusion as your asset library grows.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › New 3D Project
Step-by-step
  1. Open Unity Hub and click "New Project".
  2. Select the 3D Core template and give the project a clear name.
  3. Choose a dedicated folder that will hold Assets and Scenes.
  4. Open the Editor, then immediately save the default Scene as "MainScene".
Don't use temporary or synced folders for long-term projects.
Starter scene example (visual)
// Hierarchy after creating 3D Core project
Main Camera
Directional Light
// Save this scene as: Assets/Scenes/MainScene.unity
Key Takeaway

Establish a named project and saved scene immediately to create a reliable foundation for asset management and versioning.

screens.title: Scene View vs Game View
screens.narratorSegment: Scene View and Game View serve different purposes. Scene View is your editing workspace: you navigate freely, place and manipulate GameObjects, and compose the environment. Game View is the runtime preview produced by the active Camera, and it shows what the end user will see. A clear concrete example: if you move a Cube in Scene View, you are changing the scene; the Game View will reflect that change only when the scene is saved or the Editor runs the scene. Beginners often try to edit directly in Game View; this is a misconception because Game View is not designed for free navigation and object placement. Another difference is control: Scene View offers Transform tools — Move, Rotate, Scale — which let you snap, constrain, and position precisely. Game View shows post-processing, UI overlays, and camera perspective exactly as the player experiences it, which is why you test gameplay and camera framing there. A practical debugging tip: if an object disappears from view, double-click it in the Hierarchy to focus the Scene camera. Closing question: before you press Play, what checks would you run to ensure the Game View shows the expected camera framing and visible objects?

keyIdea.title: Edit in Scene, verify in Game
keyIdea.text: Use Scene View to build and Game View to preview runtime appearance; avoid editing in Game View.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Scene vs Game
Scene View
Editing workspace with full navigation and visual tools to place and adjust GameObjects.
  • Use Move, Rotate, and Scale handles to manipulate objects.
  • Double-click an item in Hierarchy to focus it.
  • Scene View supports snapping and orthographic views for precision.
Game View
Runtime preview rendered through the active Camera; used for testing camera framing and UI placement.
  • Shows post-processing and runtime effects not always visible in Scene view.
  • Do not edit transforms here; use Scene View for layout changes.
  • Use Game View to test input, UI, and camera framing.
Check your understanding

Before pressing Play, verify the active Camera transform, ensure visible objects have Mesh Renderers and materials, and confirm lighting is sufficient for the Game View preview.

screens.title: Hierarchy and Project windows
screens.narratorSegment: Hierarchy and Project windows provide two different but related views of your project. The Hierarchy lists the GameObjects that exist in the active scene, organized in a parent-child structure. The Project window shows every asset file in your project folder — models, textures, scripts, audio, and created materials. A concrete example: when you drag a 3D model file from the Project window into the Scene, an instance of that asset appears in the Hierarchy as a GameObject. The Hierarchy controls scene structure and parent-child transforms: a rotated parent will affect child positions. The Project window is persistent across scenes and holds canonical assets. A common beginner mistake is assuming deleting a GameObject in the Hierarchy deletes the asset; it only removes the scene instance. To permanently remove a file, delete it from the Project window. Another tip: organize your Project window with folders like Scenes, Materials, Scripts, and Prefabs to keep assets discoverable as complexity grows. Final takeaway: use Hierarchy for scene composition and Project for asset management, and remember that assets and instances are separate but connected concepts. Hierarchy and Project windows means hierarchy shows scene instances; project stores reusable asset files. they are connected but distinct.. In practical terms, where scene objects and assets live. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Hierarchy & Project
Hierarchy (scene instances)
Lists GameObjects in the current scene. Use it to arrange parent-child relationships and to focus or select objects for editing.
Parent-child relationships
Moving a parent moves its children because transforms are relative to parents.
Scene instances vs assets
Deleting an instance from Hierarchy does not remove the source asset from the Project window.
Project (asset storage)
Stores models, textures, materials, scripts, and prefabs. Organize with folders for clarity and reuse.
Concrete example
Import a 3D model into Project, then drag it into Scene. The model appears as an instance in Hierarchy while the original file stays in Project.
Key Takeaway

Keep Project well organized and treat Hierarchy as the scene’s runtime composition; they are separate layers of your project structure.

screens.title: Inspector, Components, and the Transform
screens.narratorSegment: The Inspector is where you examine and edit the properties of the selected GameObject or asset. By selecting an object in the Hierarchy, the Inspector reveals its attached Components. The Transform component is present on every GameObject and defines Position, Rotation, and Scale. Other Components, like Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer, Collider, Rigidbody, and Scripts, add shape, visibility, physics, and custom behavior. A concrete example: when you create a Cube, the Inspector shows a Transform, a Mesh Filter referencing the cube mesh, and a Mesh Renderer that controls visibility and material. If you remove the Mesh Renderer, the cube will exist in the scene but will not be drawn — a frequent cause of invisible models. A common misconception is that GameObjects themselves contain behavior; actually, behavior lives in Components. Scripts you write in C# are attached as components in the Inspector. A practical workflow: select an object, inspect the Transform, and adjust values numerically for exact placement, or use the scene tools for visual adjustment. Final takeaway: the Inspector is the primary place to configure components, and understanding the Transform plus render and physics components gives you full control over an object's presence and behavior in the scene.

keyIdea.title: Inspector drives configuration
keyIdea.text: Components attached in the Inspector give GameObjects their appearance and behavior; Transform always present.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Inspector & Components
The Transform component
Every GameObject includes Transform with Position, Rotation, and Scale values you can edit numerically or via the scene tools.
Transform:
  Position: (X: 0, Y: 0.5, Z: 0)
  Rotation: (X: 0, Y: 0, Z: 0)
  Scale:    (X: 1, Y: 1, Z: 1)
Components that affect appearance and physics
  • Mesh Filter: defines the geometry used by the object.
  • Mesh Renderer: renders the mesh using assigned materials.
  • Rigidbody and Collider: enable physics and collisions.
  • Script Components: custom behavior authored by you in C#.
If a model is invisible, check the Mesh Renderer and material assignment in the Inspector first.
Key Takeaway

Use the Inspector to attach and configure components; remember that GameObjects are containers while Components provide function and appearance.

screens.title: Manipulating GameObjects: Move, Rotate, Scale
screens.narratorSegment: Manipulating objects in 3D space is a fundamental XR skill. Unity offers three primary Transform tools: Move, Rotate, and Scale. Use the Move tool to translate objects along axes or constrained planes; use the Rotate tool for camera or object orientation; use Scale to resize objects uniformly or non-uniformly. You can operate these tools visually in Scene view or by typing precise values in the Inspector. A concrete example: create a Cube and set its Transform to Position X: 0, Y: 0.5, Z: 0 to place it on the ground plane. Then create a Sphere and set its Position X: 2, Y: 1, Z: 0 and Scale to 1.5 uniformly to make it larger. A common misconception is that scaling always preserves collider behavior; non-uniform scaling can affect physics and may require adjusting colliders or using a scaled parent container. Another pitfall is losing orientation context; use gizmo handles and the Scene camera to keep track of axes. Practice movement with snapping and use numeric inputs in the Inspector for reproducible layouts. Final takeaway: balance visual manipulation for speed with numeric values for precision, and be mindful of how parent transforms affect children.

screens.title: Common beginner mistakes and tips
screens.narratorSegment: Working in Unity as a beginner often brings predictable issues. First, forgetting to save scenes is common; always save early and often to avoid lost work. Second, invisible or placeholder models usually mean a missing Mesh Renderer or an unassigned material; check the Inspector for those components. Third, editing in Game View rather than Scene View leads to confusion because Game View is a preview and does not support the full editing toolset. Fourth, losing objects in Scene View can be resolved by double-clicking the object in the Hierarchy to focus the Scene camera. A practical tip is to maintain a folder structure in Project — Scenes, Materials, Prefabs, Scripts — so you can find files quickly as the project grows. Another subtle point: adding build modules after project setup works but interrupts flow; include necessary build support during Editor installation when possible. A misconception to avoid is assuming a missing mesh means missing asset: sometimes the mesh exists but the Mesh Renderer or material settings prevent rendering. Final suggestion: build small scenes, verify in Game View often, and use Inspector numeric values when you need exact placement. What small habit will you adopt to avoid these mistakes?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we introduce Unity as the primary tool for creating AR and VR experiences, and we orient you to the first steps you will take. Unity is a cross-platform engine used to build everything from simple AR overlays on phones to full VR worlds for headsets. You will learn what Unity Hub does, why you install the Editor with specific build support modules, and how starting with a 3D Core template gives you control as you learn. I'll show the core Editor windows — Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector — and explain how they map to tasks like placing objects, previewing a camera, and editing properties. We'll create simple geometry, attach a material, and manipulate transforms so you can feel confident moving in 3D space. This orientation matters because the early choices — which Editor version you use, which build supports you include, and whether you edit in Scene view or Game view — shape your workflow and reduce platform friction later. As a concrete example, including Android Build Support up front lets you deploy directly to many mobile AR and standalone headsets later without reinstalling. Notice a common misconception: the Game view is a preview, not the place to edit scene layout. By the end you'll know where to start, what steps to take first, and how to avoid the typical setup mistakes that cost time. How will you apply this setup to your first XR prototype?

These objectives describe the practical skills you will build. First, you will understand why Unity is preferred for AR and VR: its cross-platform editor, package ecosystem, and component model make it effective for XR prototyping and production. Second, you will learn to navigate Unity Hub and create a 3D Core project, which sets up the project folder and initial scene. Third, you will identify the Editor's core windows — Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector — and know which window to use for each task. Fourth, you will practice manipulating GameObjects with translation, rotation, and scaling, and you'll understand how GameObjects and Components relate so you can attach behaviors through scripts or built-in modules. Each objective is framed for action: you will demonstrate these skills by creating a simple 3D scene and applying transforms and materials. A common misconception is that Unity's Editor is only for games; in fact, the same tools map directly to AR overlays and VR experiences. By the end you will not only know what each window does, but also why it matters and how to apply these capabilities to a real XR prototype.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice and troubleshooting. You will practice creating a Cube, Sphere, and Cylinder and setting their Transform properties exactly as shown. You'll learn to create a Material asset and apply colors using the Inspector. As you do these tasks, notice how the Hierarchy lists created GameObjects, the Project window holds the Material asset, and the Inspector reveals the Transform and Renderer properties. Understanding this mapping from action to window reduces mistakes when you import complex models later. A common beginner error is modifying objects in Game view; save edits happen in Scene view and you confirm results in Game view. Another common issue is missing rendering: if an imported model appears as a placeholder, check for a missing Mesh Renderer component or an unassigned material. These practice outcomes are deliberately concrete so you can test them quickly. After completing the activity, you should be able to explain where assets live, how to attach a material, and how to adjust transforms so objects appear where you expect them in the scene.

Unity is a cross-platform game engine with an editor designed for building interactive 3D content. Saying that Unity is 'good for XR' means it provides a unified workflow for creating scenes, composing assets, and deploying to multiple targets. Practically, that matters because AR and VR projects must run on devices with different operating systems, input systems, and performance constraints. For example, you might prototype an AR overlay on Android and later target a standalone headset. Unity's package ecosystem and community assets accelerate that transition. A concrete example: if you add Android Build Support during Editor installation, you can deploy the same scene to many mobile devices without reinstalling the Editor. A common misconception is that Unity is only for games. In reality, its component-based architecture, render pipeline, and XR toolkits support applications across visualization, simulation, training, and spatial UI. Another pitfall is assuming Unity automates platform differences; it does not. You still configure input, performance budgets, and platform-specific build settings. Key takeaway: Unity gives you a consistent authoring environment and reusable components, but you must make explicit platform choices early to avoid reinstalling or incompatible builds. Consider: which target device do you plan to test on first, and what build support will that require?

Unity Hub is a small desktop manager that organizes Unity Editor versions, project folders, and learning resources. Think of it as a control center: you use it to install specific Editor versions and add modules like Android Build Support or Universal Windows Platform support. The process begins with installing Unity Hub, signing in, and selecting an Editor version to install. When you choose an Editor, include the build support modules for the platforms you expect to target. For example, if you plan to build mobile AR or deploy to a Quest headset, include Android Build Support up front. A concrete step: after Hub installation, click New Project, select the 3D Core template, give the project a name, and choose a location. A frequent beginner mistake is installing a single Editor version without necessary modules and then being blocked when trying to build. You can add modules later, but it interrupts flow. Another misconception is that the Hub is optional; while you can run the Editor standalone, Hub provides version control and project organization that prevents version mismatch problems. Takeaway: use Hub to create a named project tied to a specific Editor version and include the right build modules at install time so you avoid reinstalling later.

Creating a new 3D Core project is your first hands-on step. From Unity Hub, click New Project and choose the 3D Core template; this template sets up a blank scene with default lighting and a main camera so you can focus on objects and transforms. Name the project clearly and choose a folder where you want your assets to live. After creating the project, Unity will open the Editor and present a Scene with a Main Camera and a Directional Light already in the Hierarchy. A concrete example: name your project "XR_First_Scene" and pick a dedicated folder in your Documents area to avoid mixing experimental files. A common beginner error is creating projects in temporary or synced folders that cause file locking or version issues. Also, avoid enabling experimental preview packages during initial setup; they can introduce instability. After the project is created, save the default scene (File > Save Scene) and give it a name, for example "MainScene". This habit prevents losing changes and makes your project portable. Final takeaway: a named project with a saved initial scene and appropriate folder structure prevents confusion as your asset library grows.

Scene View and Game View serve different purposes. Scene View is your editing workspace: you navigate freely, place and manipulate GameObjects, and compose the environment. Game View is the runtime preview produced by the active Camera, and it shows what the end user will see. A clear concrete example: if you move a Cube in Scene View, you are changing the scene; the Game View will reflect that change only when the scene is saved or the Editor runs the scene. Beginners often try to edit directly in Game View; this is a misconception because Game View is not designed for free navigation and object placement. Another difference is control: Scene View offers Transform tools — Move, Rotate, Scale — which let you snap, constrain, and position precisely. Game View shows post-processing, UI overlays, and camera perspective exactly as the player experiences it, which is why you test gameplay and camera framing there. A practical debugging tip: if an object disappears from view, double-click it in the Hierarchy to focus the Scene camera. Closing question: before you press Play, what checks would you run to ensure the Game View shows the expected camera framing and visible objects?

Hierarchy and Project windows provide two different but related views of your project. The Hierarchy lists the GameObjects that exist in the active scene, organized in a parent-child structure. The Project window shows every asset file in your project folder — models, textures, scripts, audio, and created materials. A concrete example: when you drag a 3D model file from the Project window into the Scene, an instance of that asset appears in the Hierarchy as a GameObject. The Hierarchy controls scene structure and parent-child transforms: a rotated parent will affect child positions. The Project window is persistent across scenes and holds canonical assets. A common beginner mistake is assuming deleting a GameObject in the Hierarchy deletes the asset; it only removes the scene instance. To permanently remove a file, delete it from the Project window. Another tip: organize your Project window with folders like Scenes, Materials, Scripts, and Prefabs to keep assets discoverable as complexity grows. Final takeaway: use Hierarchy for scene composition and Project for asset management, and remember that assets and instances are separate but connected concepts. Hierarchy and Project windows means hierarchy shows scene instances; project stores reusable asset files. they are connected but distinct.. In practical terms, where scene objects and assets live. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Inspector is where you examine and edit the properties of the selected GameObject or asset. By selecting an object in the Hierarchy, the Inspector reveals its attached Components. The Transform component is present on every GameObject and defines Position, Rotation, and Scale. Other Components, like Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer, Collider, Rigidbody, and Scripts, add shape, visibility, physics, and custom behavior. A concrete example: when you create a Cube, the Inspector shows a Transform, a Mesh Filter referencing the cube mesh, and a Mesh Renderer that controls visibility and material. If you remove the Mesh Renderer, the cube will exist in the scene but will not be drawn — a frequent cause of invisible models. A common misconception is that GameObjects themselves contain behavior; actually, behavior lives in Components. Scripts you write in C# are attached as components in the Inspector. A practical workflow: select an object, inspect the Transform, and adjust values numerically for exact placement, or use the scene tools for visual adjustment. Final takeaway: the Inspector is the primary place to configure components, and understanding the Transform plus render and physics components gives you full control over an object's presence and behavior in the scene.

Manipulating objects in 3D space is a fundamental XR skill. Unity offers three primary Transform tools: Move, Rotate, and Scale. Use the Move tool to translate objects along axes or constrained planes; use the Rotate tool for camera or object orientation; use Scale to resize objects uniformly or non-uniformly. You can operate these tools visually in Scene view or by typing precise values in the Inspector. A concrete example: create a Cube and set its Transform to Position X: 0, Y: 0.5, Z: 0 to place it on the ground plane. Practice movement with snapping and use numeric inputs in the Inspector for reproducible layouts. Final takeaway: balance visual manipulation for speed with numeric values for precision, and be mindful of how parent transforms affect children.
